intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that Stickler syndrome type VI (STL6) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL9A3 gene on chromosome 20q13.3.

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI (STL6) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the COL9A3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: 19 patients have been reported to date, with STL caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in genes that encode for the three chains of type IX collagen: COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3.
checks.explanation: Recessive COL9A3-related STL due to homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations.

checks.claim: The COL9A3 gene is located on chromosome 20q13.3.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we describe the first autosomal recessive Stickler family due to loss of function mutations (c.1176_1198del, p.Gln393Cysfs*25) of COL9A3 gene.
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene the paper names; the abstract itself does not give 20q13.3.

paragraphs.text: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder caused by biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the COL9A3 gene, which encodes the alpha-3 chain of type IX collagen. The features seen in all affected individuals are early-onset, moderate to profound, often progressive sensorineural hearing loss and high myopia. Vitreoretinal degeneration, retinal detachment, and cataract occur in some patients. Skeletal involvement varies and includes epiphyseal or spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, bowing of the long bones, and early-onset arthropathy. Cleft palate has not been reported (Faletra et al., 2014; Hanson-Kahn et al., 2018; Markova et al., 2021; Rad et al., 2022).

checks.claim: Stickler syndrome type VI is an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Here, we describe the first autosomal recessive Stickler family due to loss of function mutations (c.1176_1198del, p.Gln393Cysfs*25) of COL9A3 gene.
checks.explanation: Recessive Stickler syndrome caused by a collagen gene is described.

paragraphs.text: Faletra et al. (2014) described the first family with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome caused by loss-of-function mutation in the COL9A3 gene. Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) summarized the family, which had 3 affected sibs. Their features were moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss, high myopia, normal vitreous, midface hypoplasia, tibial rotation, mild irregularities of the capital femoral and metacarpal epiphyses, and pes planus. The sibs also had moderate to severe intellectual disability. According to Rad et al. (2022), the family was Moroccan and the parents were first cousins. The patients were 4, 11, and 16 years old.

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) reported a boy whose parents were third cousins from India. He failed his newborn hearing screen. At 5 months, audiologic evaluation showed moderate to severe sensorineural hearing loss on the right and severe sensorineural hearing loss on the left, from 250 through 4,000 Hz. The hearing loss remained stable. A CT scan of the temporal bones at 7 months was negative apart from mild enlargement of the vestibular aqueducts. He had no myopia at 5 months. By 2 years, he had myopia of -6.75 OD and -8 OS, which progressed to -10.75 OD and -11.25 OS by 12 years. No vitreous abnormalities were noted. Femoral and tibial bowing were present at birth. Radiographs at 6 years showed slightly flattened proximal femoral epiphyses, flattening of the acetabula, irregularity of the medial distal femoral epiphyses, and mild platyspondyly with irregular vertebral endplates. Growth parameters were in the normal range. Intelligence was normal, and early speech delay was attributed to the hearing loss. Autoimmune hypothyroidism was identified at 10 years. His parents and older sister were reported to be unaffected.

paragraphs.text: Nixon et al. (2019) described 2 patients from 1 family with recessive Stickler syndrome due to COL9A3 variants, as part of a study of 4 families with type IX collagen defects. All patients in the study were highly myopic, had congenital megalophthalmos with abnormal, hypoplastic vitreous gel, and had sensorineural hearing loss. One patient had severe arthropathy. Markova et al. (2021) and Rad et al. (2022) gave further details of the COL9A3 family. The older sib had a refraction of -23 D in each eye at age 20 years, as well as severe arthropathy of the shoulders and hips, scoliosis that had been treated surgically, and narrowing of the knee joint spaces. This patient used a wheelchair. The younger sib did not have these skeletal findings. Rad et al. (2022) noted that Nixon et al. (2019) had observed mild Stickler phenotypes in carrier parents.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) reported a boy from a nonconsanguineous Russian family. The pregnancy was complicated by oligohydramnios and fetal growth retardation. At 1 month, he had hip dysplasia on ultrasound and bilateral absence of ossification centers. Congenital high bilateral myopia was found at 3 months. Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss of grade 3 to 4 was diagnosed at 11 months, and auditory thresholds were 75 dB on the right and 70 dB on the left. Speech development was delayed. Ophthalmic examination showed peripheral pigment rearrangement, small whitish dystrophic foci at the periphery, multiple vitreous floaters, and a preretinal membrane in the right eye. The electroretinogram was normal. Radiographs at 1 and 3 years showed spina bifida occulta of the sacral vertebrae, mild platyspondyly, kyphosis with the apex at T11, flattened and irregular femoral heads with broadened, shortened necks, coxa valga, and flattened distal femoral epiphyses, which were consistent with mild spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. At 2 years and 5 months, height was 88 cm (25th to 50th percentile). He had genu valgum, a waddling gait, rapid fatigability, and pain in the lower limb joints from 3 years of age. He also had a slightly flattened nasal bridge, small nose, mild midface hypoplasia, high palate, lumbar lordosis, limited hip abduction, long fingers, and planovalgus foot deformity. The authors considered that this case widened the phenotype to include early-onset arthropathy and vitreoretinal degeneration.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) reported 5 affected individuals from 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families. In each family the parents were first cousins. The proband of family 1 was a 28-year-old woman. She had high myopia and vitreoretinal degeneration with empty vitreous, multiple lattice degenerations, and retinal pigmentary changes. Optical coherence tomography showed retinal detachment. She also had severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss and knee pain, but skeletal examination and x-rays were normal. In family 2, 2 sibs aged 65 and 57 years had high myopia and advanced vitreoretinal degeneration with recurrent rhegmatogenous retinal detachments that required multiple surgeries. Both were left with severely reduced vision or blindness. They also had cataract, profound progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and herniated cervical discs. In family 3, a boy aged 11.8 years and his sister aged 3.1 years had myopia, congenital moderate to severe progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia. They also had pes planus, a depressed nasal bridge, and anteverted nares. Midface hypoplasia and downslanting palpebral fissures were more pronounced in the girl. The boy had knee pain, genu valgum, bowed tibiae, short metacarpals, and flattened femoral heads. None of the patients had short stature, cleft palate, or intellectual disability. Rad et al. (2022) concluded that high myopia and moderate to severe hearing loss were consistent features, whereas skeletal findings were more variable. The older patients in family 2 had fewer skeletal findings than the young patients in family 3.

paragraphs.text: Hanson-Kahn et al. (2018) used exome sequencing to study a boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome born to consanguineous Indian parents. They found that he was homozygous for a 1-bp duplication (c.650dupC) in exon 13 of the COL9A3 gene, which was predicted to cause a frameshift and premature termination. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation and showed that both parents and an unaffected sib were heterozygous. The mutation was not found in public SNP databases. Earlier targeted testing of COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2, and specific exons of COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3 had been negative.

paragraphs.text: Markova et al. (2021) studied a Russian boy with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome using targeted next-generation sequencing of 166 genes associated with skeletal disorders. They found 2 nonsense mutations in the COL9A3 gene: c.268C-T (Arg90Ter) in exon 5 and c.1729C-T (Arg577Ter) in exon 30. Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutations, and segregation analysis showed that they were in trans. The healthy sibs did not carry pathogenic COL9A3 variants. This was the first patient reported with compound heterozygous rather than homozygous COL9A3 mutations.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) performed exome sequencing on the probands of 3 unrelated consanguineous Iranian families with autosomal recessive Stickler syndrome. Each proband was homozygous for a different novel loss-of-function mutation in COL9A3. The family 1 proband had a 10-bp deletion (c.107_116del) that caused a frameshift in exon 2 (Pro36ArgfsTer49); this variant had an allele frequency of 0.00001390 in gnomAD. The family 2 proband had a nonsense mutation, c.1204C-T (Arg402Ter), in exon 23. The family 3 proband had a 1-bp deletion (c.355delC) in exon 7 (Leu119SerfsTer9). The last 2 variants were not found in public databases. Segregation analysis by Sanger sequencing was performed in available family members.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous 1-bp deletion (c.355delC) in exon 7 of the COL9A3 gene in the proband of a consanguineous Iranian family with Stickler syndrome type VI. The family had 2 affected sibs. The deletion caused a frameshift, given as Leu119SerfsTer9 in the text and Leu119SerfsTer10 in the table. The variant was not reported in public databases.

checks.claim: Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous 1-bp deletion (c.355delC) in exon 7 of the COL9A3 gene in the proband of a consanguineous Iranian family with Stickler syndrome type VI.
checks.evidence_quote: the proband in Family 3 showed a one base pair deletion in COL9A3 [c.355delC, p.(Leu119Serfs*9)] in exon 7.

checks.claim: The Iranian family with COL9A3 c.355delC had 2 affected sibs.
checks.evidence_quote: Family 3 presented with two affected and two healthy children from first cousin parents.

checks.claim: Rad et al. (2022) gave the frameshift caused by COL9A3 c.355delC as Leu119SerfsTer9 in the text and Leu119SerfsTer10 in the table.
checks.evidence_quote: [c.355delC, p.(Leu119Serfs*9)] in exon 7.

checks.claim: The COL9A3 c.355delC variant was not reported in public databases.
checks.evidence_quote: Both variants have not been reported in public databases.

paragraphs.text: Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.1204C-T transition in exon 23 of the COL9A3 gene, resulting in an arg402-to-ter (R402X) substitution, in the proband of a consanguineous Iranian family with Stickler syndrome type VI. The family had 2 affected sibs, aged 65 and 57 years. The variant was not reported in public databases.

checks.claim: Rad et al. (2022) used exome sequencing to identify a homozygous c.1204C-T transition in exon 23 of the COL9A3 gene, resulting in an R402X substitution, in the proband of a consanguineous Iranian family with Stickler syndrome type VI.
checks.evidence_quote: The proband in family 2 disclosed a COL9A3 nonsense variant (c.1204C > T, p.(Arg402*), rs989413835) in exon 23
checks.explanation: Homozygous, found by exome sequencing; first-cousin Iranian family.
